conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode unless noted; trend line and swing-pivot detection are assumed as primitives (trendLine.valueAt(n), swing high/low finder) even though the chapter's prose never gives their construction

candidates.name: TrendLineBreak
candidates.quote: a countertrend move (a reversal) that is strong enough to break the trend line and usually the moving average
candidates.description: Primitive: the close has broken beyond the current trend line (projected from swing pivots) by at least a margin, marking a countertrend move strong enough to be a candidate reversal signal. Long side: bear trend line broken from above (close falls below it) while the standing trend is a bear trend, signalling a possible bullish reversal.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context classification, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and trend-line projection before a break can be tested

notes: Chapter 2 (V02-10 BearTrendLineBreak / V02-19 TrendLineBreakByMargin) already define close variants of this; redefined here as the local primitive this chapter's candidates depend on. Dedup pass should merge.

candidates.name: TrendLineBreakReachesEma
candidates.quote: If the break of the trend line is not even strong enough to reach the moving average, it is usually not strong enough to reverse the trend, so do not begin looking for a trend reversal just yet.
candidates.description: A trend-line break only counts as a meaningful reversal sign if the same countertrend move also closes beyond the moving average; a break that stays above (bull case) / below (bear case) the EMA should be ignored and the trader should keep taking only with-trend setups.

complexity.reason: depends on the trend-line primitive plus an EMA read

notes: Overlaps V02-17 CloseAboveEmaByMargin conceptually; kept as the AND of trend-line break and EMA break since the book states them as a joint requirement.

candidates.name: TestOvershootsPriorSwingExtreme
candidates.quote: The test may overshoot the old extreme as in the case of a lower low in a new bull trend or a higher high in a new bear trend... Overshoots are, strictly speaking, the final leg of the old trend.
candidates.description: After a trend-line break, the countertrend test of the old trend's extreme makes a NEW extreme beyond the prior swing high/low (e.g., a lower low while a bull reversal is developing). This overshoot is classified as the final leg of the old trend rather than the reversal itself, so a fresh pullback and second leg should be required before treating it as the reversal signal.

complexity.reason: needs the prior swing extreme identified by pivot detection

candidates.name: TestUndershootsPriorSwingExtreme
candidates.quote: or it may undershoot it with a higher low in a new bull trend or a lower high in a new bear trend... An undershoot is the pullback from the first leg in the new trend.
candidates.description: The countertrend test stops short of the prior swing extreme (e.g., a higher low without reaching the prior low). Brooks classifies this as the pullback within the new trend's first leg, i.e., closer to a completed reversal than an overshoot is.

complexity.reason: needs the prior swing extreme identified by pivot detection

candidates.name: SecondLegConfirmationAfterTest
candidates.quote: Since the countertrend move after a trend line break usually has at least two legs, if a bull reversal has a higher low for the test of the bear low, it will also be the start of the second leg.
candidates.description: If the test undershoot (higher low / lower high) forms, treat it as already the START of the second leg -- the reversal is closer to confirmed. If the test overshoots (lower low / higher high) instead, require a pullback and then a further push beyond that overshoot (the actual second leg) before treating the reversal as confirmed.

complexity.reason: leg counting from pivots, plus branching on which of two prior candidates fired

notes: Brooks is describing a discretionary heuristic (which leg you are in), not a crisp entry trigger; encoded here as a best-effort mechanization.

candidates.name: MajorTrendReversalFourPartSetup
candidates.quote: Four things are needed for a major trend reversal: 1. A trend... 2. A countertrend move... that breaks the trend line... 3. A test of the trend's extreme, and then a second reversal... 4. The second reversal going far enough for there to be a consensus that the trend has reversed.
candidates.description: The book's full definition of a major trend reversal: an established trend, a trend-line break reaching the EMA, a test of the trend's extreme (over- or undershoot), and a second reversal that goes far enough to convince most traders the trend has changed. Item 4 ("far enough for consensus") is explicitly a design decision, not a bar-level test.
candidates.pseudocode: trendExists && trendLineBroken(V03-02) && testOfExtreme(V03-03_or_V03-04) && secondReversalConfirmed(V03-05) && secondReversalMagnitude >= consensusThreshold

complexity.reason: requires a design decision for what counts as "far enough for consensus" (item 4); the rest chains hard sub-candidates

notes: This is the chapter's organizing definition; the authoring pass should treat items 1-3 as the composable, gradeable parts and flag item 4 as out of scope for a mechanical rule.

candidates.name: TestExtendsTooFarWithoutPullback
candidates.quote: if the move to a higher high goes five or more bars above the old bull high, traders usually should begin the process from the beginning and wait for another break below a bull trend line
candidates.description: If, after a trend-line break, the rally (test of the old high) closes at least N bars above the prior swing high without any pullback, treat the test as a successful breakout / trend continuation rather than a reversal setup, and stop looking for a short until there is another trend-line break.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (filter that blocks a countertrend entry)

complexity.reason: a persisting bar counter since the breakout plus a fixed prior-extreme comparison

candidates.name: SteepChannelTestBlocksReversal
candidates.quote: If the rally is in a very tight, steep channel with no pullbacks and very little overlap between consecutive bars... the odds are increased that the bull trend will resume, despite that earlier strong sell-off and breakout below the bull trend line.
candidates.description: If the test move back toward the prior extreme is a steep, low-overlap channel (little bar-to-bar overlap, no pullbacks), treat it as likely trend continuation and do not take the reversal trade; wait for a breakout of that channel and a pullback first.

complexity.reason: "steep, low-overlap channel" has no numeric definition in the text; needs a chosen slope/overlap metric before coding

notes: Recurs across three separate chart examples (bars 12-13 AAPL, bars 11-14 GS, bar 6-7 GS); clearly an important Brooks concept even though it resists a crisp default.

candidates.name: OppositeLargeSpikePairSignalsRange
candidates.quote: Spikes like this are common in trends. However, the test of the bottom of a channel usually leads to a trading range as it did here. Big up + big down = big confusion = trading range.
candidates.description: When a large trend bar (or short spike) in one direction is immediately followed by a comparably large trend bar in the opposite direction, expect the market to enter a trading range rather than continue trending; suppress strong-trend assumptions after such a pair.
candidates.pseudocode: (high[1] - low[1]) >= bigBarAtrMultiple * atr[1] && (high[0] - low[0]) >= bigBarAtrMultiple * atr[0] && ((close[1] > open[1]) != (close[0] > open[0]))

complexity.reason: an ATR read plus a two-bar range/direction comparison

notes: Overlaps the topic of Chapter 4 (climactic reversals: a spike followed by a spike); flag for dedup with that chapter's mining.

candidates.name: ConsecutiveTrendBarsFadeSignal
candidates.quote: Once he saw five or more consecutive bear bars, he could then place a limit order to short at the high of the prior bar, expecting the first reversal attempt after a strong bear spike to fail.
candidates.description: After N or more consecutive same-direction trend bars (a spike), place a with-trend entry at a limit price at the prior bar's extreme, betting that the first countertrend reversal attempt will fail. Long side: after N consecutive bull trend bars, buy at a limit at the low of the prior bar.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the high/low of the prior bar (mechanized here as a resting limit checked against next bar's range)

complexity.reason: a persistent same-direction trend-bar counter plus a limit-fill check

notes: Distinct from ConsecutiveUpBars in the main catalog, which tests close>open streaks for a momentum continuation entry; this is a countertrend-fade entry placed WITH the established trend after a bar-count streak of true trend bars.

candidates.name: BreakoutWithoutPullbackContinuation
candidates.quote: If the market goes up far enough above the breakout to enable a trader to make at least a profitable scalp before there is a pullback, then assume that there was mostly new buying at the high.
candidates.description: After a breakout above a prior swing high, if price moves at least X ticks/points beyond the breakout level within the first few bars without any pullback, classify the move as new with-trend buying (continuation) rather than a reversal setup.

complexity.reason: a fixed-distance, fixed-bar-window comparison off a recorded breakout level

notes: Close in spirit to V02-04 SpikeWithoutPullback; kept separate because this one is keyed to a specific breakout level rather than a general spike.

candidates.name: SidewaysAfterBreakoutProfitTaking
candidates.quote: If it goes sideways, assume that there was profit taking and that the bulls are looking to buy again a little lower.
candidates.description: After a breakout above a prior high, if price goes sideways (a tight, overlapping range) for several bars rather than extending or reversing hard, classify this as profit-taking and expect a pullback buy rather than a reversal or clean continuation.

complexity.reason: "goes sideways" has no Brooks-given numeric threshold; needs a chosen range/ATR ratio

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutReversalAfterNewExtreme
candidates.quote: If the market reverses down hard, assume that the strong bears dominated at the new high and that the market will likely trade down for at least a couple of legs and at least 10 bars.
candidates.description: After a breakout above a prior swing high, if price closes back below the breakout level within a few bars, treat it as a strong countertrend (short) signal, mechanized as the close-then-next-open stop entry below the breakout level.
candidates.pseudocode: highestHigh(sinceBreakoutBars) > breakoutLevel && close[0] < breakoutLevel && barsSinceBreakout <= confirmBars
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop below the breakout level, mechanized as close back below the level then next bar's open

complexity.reason: recorded breakout level plus a bar-window close-back-through test

notes: Near-duplicate of V02-22 FailedBreakoutBelowSwingLow; kept because this chapter states it as a failure of a NEW-HIGH breakout specifically (not just any swing low break) and pairs it with an expected minimum move (10 bars, two legs) that V02-22 does not carry.

candidates.name: PullbacksWidenAsTrendMatures
candidates.quote: Once a strong bull trend begins to have pullbacks that are relatively large, the pullbacks... behave more like trading ranges than bull flags... A new high is now a breakout attempt above a trading range, and the odds are that it will fail.
candidates.description: As a trend matures, its pullbacks grow larger/more range-like relative to earlier pullbacks in the same trend; once pullback size crosses some multiple of the trend's earlier average pullback, treat new breakouts in the trend direction as trading-range breakouts (lower odds of follow-through) rather than flag breakouts.

complexity.reason: requires defining and tracking "pullback size" over the trend's history and a threshold for what counts as widened; no number given

candidates.name: IiPatternRequiresPriorTrendLineBreak
candidates.quote: Bar 5 was an ii pattern, which is often a reversal pattern (but it needs an earlier trend line break)... Since there was no prior trend line break, the only breakout that was a valid entry was a bear breakout.
candidates.description: An ii (inside-inside) pattern's breakout only counts as a valid countertrend reversal setup if a trend-line break already occurred earlier in the move; without a prior break, only the with-trend breakout of the ii pattern is a valid entry.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (filter on which side of an ii breakout is valid)

complexity.reason: gates an existing pattern (ii, assumed defined elsewhere) on the trend-line-break primitive

notes: The ii pattern itself is not defined in this chapter (it is a bar-pattern primitive from the Trends volume); this candidate only captures the added gating condition.

candidates.name: StrongReversalBarReversesHighsAndCloses
candidates.quote: It closed above the close of every bar since bar 6 and its high was above the high of every bar since the bar after bar 6. The more highs and closes that a strong bull bar reverses, the stronger the bull reversal.
candidates.description: A reversal bar's strength is measured by how many consecutive prior bars it reverses on BOTH counts at once: its close exceeds the close of each of the last N bars, and its high exceeds the high of each of the last N-1 bars. The count N is itself the strength score.
candidates.pseudocode: barsReversedByClose = count(k=1..K : close[0] > close[k]); barsReversedByHigh = count(k=1..K : high[0] > high[k]); reversalStrength = min(barsReversedByClose, barsReversedByHigh)

complexity.reason: two running comparisons against a lookback window to produce a joint count

notes: V02-33/V02-34 already define the close-only and high-only versions separately; this chapter restates them jointly (the AND/min of both) as the actual strength measure Brooks describes.

candidates.name: BreakevenAfterFourBarRallyAboveEma
candidates.quote: The traders who bought the bar 7 two-legged higher low either had a small loss if they held until their protective stop was hit, or they got out around breakeven if they moved their stop to breakeven after a four-bar rally above the moving average.
candidates.description: Once a long position has stayed above the moving average for N consecutive bars since entry, move the protective stop to the entry price (breakeven). Mirrored for shorts (N consecutive closes below the EMA).
candidates.book_order_type: stop-loss order moved to entry price

complexity.reason: a persistent since-entry bar counter conditioned on an EMA comparison

notes: V02-16 BreakevenStop already exists as a primitive; this is a specific trigger variant (4-bar EMA-holding rally) worth flagging for the authoring pass to compare against.

candidates.name: RetracementDepthRewardRiskGate
candidates.quote: Once a pullback rallies to above 50 percent, the chance of the bear resuming becomes less... Once the probability is 50 percent or less, traders will need more of a reward if they are going to short.
candidates.description: Size the minimum acceptable reward:risk ratio for a countertrend entry based on how deep the pullback has retraced into the prior swing: at a retracement of roughly 50% require at least a 1:1 reward:risk to the swing's test target, and at deeper retracements (around 61.8-67%) require at least 2:1.
candidates.pseudocode: retracementFraction = (entryPrice - swingLow) / (swingHigh - swingLow); requiredRR = (retracementFraction <= shallowRetracement) ? 1.0 : deepRewardRiskRatio; (targetPrice - entryPrice) / (entryPrice - stopPrice) >= requiredRR

complexity.reason: needs the swing high/low of the leg being retraced plus a computed target and stop before the ratio can be checked

notes: Brooks is explicitly skeptical that Fibonacci levels are precise ("probably lost value now that trading has become so computerized"); the mechanizable content is the reward:risk-scales-with-depth heuristic, not a specific 61.8% level.

rejected.quote: An average setup has about a 40 percent chance of leading to a profitable swing, a 30 percent chance of a small loss, and a 30 percent chance of a small profit.
rejected.reason: an aggregate historical win-rate statistic, not a condition decidable from bars at signal time

rejected.quote: Bar 19 was obviously caused by some news event (it was the 2010 Flash Crash), but that is not important.
rejected.reason: attributes the move to a news event; the engine has no news/order-flow input and Brooks himself says it does not matter

rejected.quote: it is usually too difficult to read a second chart and place orders this quickly, and you would likely make more money if you just traded the 5 minute trend
rejected.reason: discretionary advice about which chart/timeframe to watch, not a bar-level test

chapter_summary: Chapter 3 defines the major trend reversal as trend + trend-line break (reaching the EMA) + a test of the trend's extreme (over- or undershoot) + a second reversal large enough for consensus, then spends most of its length on trader psychology (why institutions buy/sell at each stage) and seven fully worked chart examples (AAPL 5-min/daily, ES 5/3/1-min, GS 15-min) walking that framework and Chapter 2's primitives (trend-line breaks, EMA gaps, breakout pullbacks, double tops/bottoms, ii patterns, ADX-like channel steepness) through real setups. Genuinely new mechanizable material beyond Chapter 2 is the test-overshoot-vs-undershoot leg classification (V03-03/04/05), the 'test extends too far / too steep a channel = continuation not reversal' filters (V03-07/08), the consecutive-trend-bar fade entry (V03-10), the joint high+close reversal-strength score (V03-16, a straightforward composite of V02-33/34), a concrete breakeven-stop trigger (V03-17), and the retracement-depth-scaled reward:risk gate (V03-18). Several ideas (steep-channel test, sideways-after-breakout, pullback widening with trend maturity) are flagged 'research' because Brooks gives no numeric threshold at all. The 'big up + big down = trading range' idea (V03-09) anticipates Chapter 4's climactic-reversal topic and should be deduped against it.
